data.name: groupAir.ToolTip
data.value: Properties of the air at the given temperature and humidity. Saturation vapour pressure uses the Magnus formula (Alduchov and Eskridge coefficients, 1996): error below 0.4 % from −40 to +50 °C. Air pressure is taken as standard, 1013 hPa.

data.name: labelTemperatureCaption.ToolTip
data.value: Room air temperature, °C. It sets how much water the air can hold: up to 17.2 g/m³ at +20 °C, but up to 30.3 g/m³ at +30 °C. So the same water gives a different relative humidity at a different temperature: the dehumidifier, warming the room, lowers it even before it collects any water. “From dehumidifier” fills in its reading.

data.name: numericTemperature.ToolTip
data.value: Room air temperature, °C. It sets how much water the air can hold: up to 17.2 g/m³ at +20 °C, but up to 30.3 g/m³ at +30 °C. So the same water gives a different relative humidity at a different temperature: the dehumidifier, warming the room, lowers it even before it collects any water. “From dehumidifier” fills in its reading.

data.name: labelHumidityCaption.ToolTip
data.value: Relative humidity, %: how much water the air holds compared with the most it can hold at this temperature. 100 % means saturated: the air cannot hold more, the excess condenses as dew. Change it and the absolute humidity is recalculated at the same temperature.

data.name: numericHumidity.ToolTip
data.value: Relative humidity, %: how much water the air holds compared with the most it can hold at this temperature. 100 % means saturated: the air cannot hold more, the excess condenses as dew. Change it and the absolute humidity is recalculated at the same temperature.

data.name: labelWaterCaption.ToolTip
data.value: Absolute humidity: grams of water per cubic metre of air. Unlike relative humidity, it does not change when the air warms up or cools down, which is why the forecast is computed in it. You can enter it yourself — the relative humidity is then recalculated at the same temperature.

data.name: numericWater.ToolTip
data.value: Absolute humidity: grams of water per cubic metre of air. Unlike relative humidity, it does not change when the air warms up or cools down, which is why the forecast is computed in it. You can enter it yourself — the relative humidity is then recalculated at the same temperature.

data.name: buttonFromDevice.ToolTip
data.value: Fill in the temperature, humidity and target that the dehumidifier is showing now. The target is not taken in laundry drying mode — that mode has none. If the dehumidifier is not connected, the fields stay as they are.

data.name: labelDewCaption.ToolTip
data.value: Dew point: the temperature this air must be cooled to for water to condense out of it. Windows, walls or pipes colder than the dew point collect condensation, and in time mould. A compressor dehumidifier works exactly so: it chills its coil below the dew point and collects the drops.

labelOtherCaption.ToolTip
data.value: What the relative humidity becomes if this air (the same water per kilogram of air) is warmed or cooled to another temperature: by a cold window, in a basement, at night, outdoors. Above 100 % means the excess water would condense as dew at that temperature.

data.name: groupRoom.ToolTip
data.value: How much water to remove from the room to reach the target at the same temperature.

data.name: labelVolumeCaption.ToolTip
data.value: Room volume, m³: floor area × ceiling height; 15 m² with a 2.7 m ceiling is about 40 m³. If the doors are open, include the adjoining rooms: they share the air. Remembered.

data.name: numericVolume.ToolTip
data.value: Room volume, m³: floor area × ceiling height; 15 m² with a 2.7 m ceiling is about 40 m³. If the doors are open, include the adjoining rooms: they share the air. Remembered.

data.name: labelBufferCaption.ToolTip
data.value: Buffer k: how many times more water the room holds than its air alone. Walls, furniture, fabrics and paper absorb moisture and give it back as the air dries, so drying takes longer and removes more than the volume alone suggests. 1 is an empty room with smooth walls; the more things, wood and fabrics, the larger k. “From records” estimates it best. Remembered.

data.name: numericBuffer.ToolTip

data.name: labelTargetCaption.ToolTip
data.value: Target humidity, %, at the same temperature. Used for “Water to remove”, the time to target and the capacity needed. 40…50 % is best for health.

data.name: numericTarget.ToolTip
data.value: Target humidity, %, at the same temperature. Used for “Water to remove”, the time to target and the capacity needed. 40…50 % is best for health.

data.name: labelRemoveCaption.ToolTip
data.value: How much water to remove so that the humidity drops to the target at the same temperature. The first number is the air alone: volume × the difference in absolute humidity now and at the target. The second includes the buffer (× k): roughly what the dehumidifier will collect in its tank, not counting the water that arrives from outside and from sources meanwhile.

data.name: labelRemove.ToolTip

data.name: groupForecast.ToolTip
data.value: Forecast by the room model: k·V·dρ/dt = n·V·(ρ outdoor − ρ) + S − c·(ρ − ρ min) ρ — absolute humidity, V — volume, k — buffer, n — air exchange, S — sources, c — the dehumidifier’s “effective flow” (from its rated capacity), ρ min — humidity at ≈ 35 %. Humidity approaches its limit exponentially with the time constant τ = k·V / (n·V + c). Temperature is taken as constant.

data.name: labelExchangeCaption.ToolTip
data.value: Air change rate, h⁻¹: how many times an hour the room’s air is replaced by incoming air. Closed windows and doors — about 0.1…0.5; airing or an extractor fan — 1 and more. If the air outside is drier, air exchange helps drying; if it is more humid, it hinders. “From records” estimates it best. Remembered.

data.name: labelOutdoorCaption.ToolTip
data.value: Temperature and relative humidity where the incoming air comes from: outdoors, a stairwell, the next room. The absolute humidity of the inflow is taken from them. Outdoor air, even damp, brings little water when cold: 2.7 g/m³ at −5 °C and 80 %, against 9.7 g/m³ in a room at +22 °C and 50 %. Remembered.

data.name: labelSourcesCaption.ToolTip
data.value: Moisture sources in the room, g/h: breathing and skin, cooking, drying laundry, plants, an aquarium. A person at rest gives about 50 g/h; laundry drying indoors — hundreds of grams an hour. A negative number is a sink: something takes moisture away, such as a cold wall or an air conditioner. “From records” estimates them best. Remembered.

data.name: labelRatedCaption.ToolTip
data.value: Rated capacity of the dehumidifier, L/day — by the standard, at 30 °C and 80 %. In an ordinary room it removes much less: the drier and colder the air, the less, and below ≈ 35 % a compressor dehumidifier hardly dries at all. The model takes removal as proportional to (ρ − ρ at 35 %) and finds the factor from the rated point. Remembered.

data.name: buttonFromRecords.ToolTip
data.value: Refine the buffer k, air exchange and sources from all saved records. Stretches with the dehumidifier off show how fast humidity approaches equilibrium with the surroundings (n/k) and which equilibrium (hence the sources); drying stretches show how fast the dehumidifier brings it down. Room volume and rated capacity are taken from the fields — set them correctly first. Stretches shorter than 10 minutes or with an almost straight course are ignored.

data.name: labelForecast.ToolTip
data.value: Inflow — how much water an hour air exchange and sources bring at the current humidity. Removal — how much the dehumidifier takes an hour at the current humidity and temperature. Without and with the dehumidifier — what humidity the room settles at, and how fast: after τ 37 % of the way remains, after 2τ 14 %, after 3τ 5 %. To target — when the humidity reaches the target if the dehumidifier runs without pauses. Capacity needed — with a lower rated capacity the dehumidifier cannot hold the target.
